finding.claim: Subscriber-supplied callbackUrl is stored without validation and later used as the target of a server-side POST, so an attacker can make the server send requests to arbitrary internal or external hosts.
finding.source: callbackUrl parameter of subscribe() (Jobs.java:13), documented as the POST /subscribe body field (Jobs.java:12)
finding.sink: client.send(req, ...) (Jobs.java:24), with the URI from URI.create(cb) (Jobs.java:21)

trace.note: subscribe(name, callbackUrl) takes the value as-is
Stored unchanged in the static subscriptions map
notifyAll() iterates all stored callback values; runs every minute
URI.create(cb) parses the stored string with no scheme, host, or port check
client.send() connects to the attacker-chosen host; response is discarded

finding.guards_checked: None on the path. subscribe() does no validation. notifyAll() has no scheme allowlist (http/https/file/etc.), no host allowlist, no private/loopback/link-local IP block, and no connect-time address check. The shared HttpClient uses default settings, which do not follow redirects, so redirect-based escapes are not a factor here. Response bodies are discarded, so the bug is blind SSRF: it can trigger POSTs to internal services but does not return their content. Authentication on the /subscribe route is not visible in this file; if it is open to unauthenticated users, the finding is reachable without credentials.

verdict.guard_found: none. subscribe() stores callbackUrl unchanged (Jobs.java:13-14), and notifyAll() calls URI.create(cb) and client.send() with no scheme, host, or address check (Jobs.java:19-24). The only validation in the file is in thumb() (Jobs.java:30), which is a different method and does not touch the subscription path.
verdict.reason: Every trace line matches the code: the callbackUrl from the /subscribe body (per the comment at Jobs.java:12) is stored at Jobs.java:14 and POSTed to at Jobs.java:21-24 with no closing guard. The /subscribe route handler and its auth are not in this repo, so reachability by a low-privilege user rests on the comment rather than on code I could read; nothing I found makes the route admin-only. Java's HttpClient rejects non-http(s) schemes, so the realistic impact is blind SSRF to http/https targets.
